title: Replacement syntax
summary: Rewrite what a pattern finds: $1, ${name}, $0 and $$ in .NET, real refactors as find-and-replace, and computed replacements with a MatchEvaluator.

steps.title: Find, then rewrite
body: A find-and-replace has two halves. The **pattern** finds text and captures pieces of it in groups. The
**replacement** is a small template that says what to write instead, and it can refer to those groups.
In .NET (C#, PowerShell, Visual Studio) the replacement language is short:
| In the replacement | Inserts |
| `$1`, `$2` | group 1, group 2 |
| `${name}` | the named group `(?<name>...)` |
| `$0` | the whole match |
| `$$` | a literal `$` |
Everything else is literal text: the replacement is **not** a regex, so `.` and `\` mean themselves there.
Below, dates written day first are rewritten as ISO 8601 (`yyyy-MM-dd`), the format that sorts correctly as
text. Try swapping `${m}` and `${d}` in the replacement and watch the result change.

steps.prompt: The pattern `(\w+)@(\w+)\.com` with the replacement `$2:$1` runs over `mail ann@contoso.com`. What is the result?
steps.explain: Only the match is replaced: `ann@contoso.com` becomes group 2, a colon, group 1. The text around the match (`mail `) is kept as it was.

steps.title: Dates to ISO 8601
prompt: A CSV export writes dates as `dd/MM/yyyy`. The importer wants `yyyy-MM-dd`. Write the pattern **and** the
Leave ISO dates and two-digit years alone.
hints: Capture day, month and year in three groups: `(\d{2})/(\d{2})/(\d{4})`.
The replacement puts them back in the other order: `$3-$2-$1`.
steps.explain: `$3-$2-$1` writes year, month, day with dashes between. Named groups (`(?<y>\d{4})` and `${y}`) say the same thing in a way the next reader understands without counting brackets.

steps.title: $0, $$ and the digit trap
body: Three details catch people out in real refactors:
- **`$0` is the whole match.** Use it to wrap text without capturing anything: pattern `\bOPS-\d+\b`,
replacement `[$0]` turns `OPS-311` into `[OPS-311]`.
- **`$$` is a literal dollar.** A price template like `$$$0` writes a `$` and then the match.
- **A group number followed by a digit is ambiguous.** Is `$10` group 10, or group 1 and a `0`? Write
`${1}0` and nobody has to guess. Braces cost nothing, so seniors use them whenever text follows.
A reference to a group that does not exist (`$7` in a pattern with two groups) is **not** an error in .NET:
it is copied as the literal text `$7`. That is why a typo in a replacement shows up as strange output, not
as an exception. Always look at a sample of the result.
```csharp
Regex.Replace("OPS-311 is fixed", @"\bOPS-\d+\b", "[$0]");   // [OPS-311] is fixed

steps.explain: `$$` is one literal dollar, then `$0` is the match `5`. `${1}0` is group 1 (`2`) followed by a literal `0`. The last line swaps the two captured letters.

steps.title: Link every ticket key
prompt: Release notes mention ticket keys like `OPS-311`. Turn each one into a Markdown link to the tracker:
A key is 2 to 5 capital letters, a dash and digits. Write the pattern and the replacement. You need no
hints: The key pattern from module 1 works: `\b[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+\b`.
steps.explain: `$0` inserts the whole match, so there is nothing to capture. Note that running this twice would link the keys inside the links again: a replacement that is safe to run twice (idempotent) is worth designing for, for example by skipping keys that already follow a `[`.

steps.prompt: Complete the C#: turn `Lovelace, Ada` into `Ada Lovelace` with named groups.
steps.explain: In .NET a named group in the replacement is `${name}`. `$<name>` is JavaScript, `\g<name>` and `\1` are Python. `$first` without braces is copied literally in .NET.

steps.title: Reformat "Last, First"
prompt: An HR export lists people as `Last, First`, separated by semicolons. The new system wants `First Last`.
Use **named groups** `last` and `first`, and refer to them by name in the replacement.
hints: Two named groups around the comma and space: `(?<last>\w+), (?<first>\w+)`.
steps.explain: Named groups survive edits: if someone later adds a middle-name group, `${first}` still means the first name, while `$2` might silently change meaning. (Real names contain spaces, hyphens and apostrophes; for production data, `[^,;]+` is closer than `\w+`.)

steps.title: Computed replacements: MatchEvaluator
body: A replacement string can only rearrange captured text. When the new text must be **computed** (a number plus
one, a name in upper case, a mask as long as the original), pass a function instead. .NET calls it once per
match with the `Match`, and inserts whatever it returns:
```csharp
using System.Text.RegularExpressions;
// Bump every number by one: "v1.9.3" becomes "v2.10.4"
var next = Regex.Replace("v1.9.3", @"\d+", m => (int.Parse(m.Value) + 1).ToString());
// Mask card numbers, keep the last four digits
var safe = Regex.Replace(log, @"\b\d{12}(\d{4})\b", m => "************" + m.Groups[1].Value);
The lambda's type is `MatchEvaluator`. Whatever it returns is inserted **literally**: no `$` processing. That
makes it the safe choice whenever the new text comes from data, not from you.

steps.explain: The evaluator runs once per match: 1, 9 and 3 become 2, 10 and 4. In the second line `\b\w` matches the first letter of each word, and the lambda upper-cases it.

steps.title: Mask email addresses before sharing a log
prompt: Support wants to attach a log to a public bug report. Write `string MaskLocalParts(string text)` that keeps the
first character of every email's local part (the part before `@`) and replaces the rest of it with `*`, one
star per character. Domains stay as they are.
| `to: bo@x.io, cc: zed@y.dev` | `to: b*@x.io, cc: z**@y.dev` |
The local part is made of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ % + -`. The number of stars depends on the match, so use
`Regex.Replace` with a lambda. `System.Text.RegularExpressions` is already imported.
template: Dojo.Eq("ann.lee becomes a******", "mail a******@contoso.com now", MaskLocalParts("mail ann.lee@contoso.com now"));
Dojo.Eq("two addresses, each masked to its own length", "to: b*@x.io, cc: z**@y.dev", MaskLocalParts("to: bo@x.io, cc: zed@y.dev"));
Dojo.Eq("plus addressing is masked too", "from j*********@contoso.com", MaskLocalParts("from jo+billing@contoso.com"));
Dojo.Eq("text without an email is unchanged", "no email here: see the docs", MaskLocalParts("no email here: see the docs"));

require.message: Computes the replacement with a lambda (MatchEvaluator)

hints: Capture the local part and require the `@` after it: `@"([A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+)@"`.
In the lambda: `var local = m.Groups[1].Value; return local[0] + new string('*', local.Length - 1) + "@";`
